newsitem.title: UK: British Gas drops on Norwegian import threat.
newsitem.headline: British Gas drops on Norwegian import threat.

text.p: Shares in British Gas Plc dropped on Monday to a near three-month low as a report of possible imports of Norwegian natural gas added to the downward pressure on the stock from last week's row with regulator Ofgas, analysts said.
The stock was down 4p at 183-1/2 by 1002 GMT in heavy trading of 4.2 million shares, making a loss of 17p since last Wednesday's close.

A report in the Financial Times said the UK government had reopened talks to allow imports of Norwegian natural gas, ensuring plentiful cheap supplies as Britain prepares to open its domestic market to full competition by 1998.

"Any more gas coming in will depress prices when what British Gas needs is higher prices," said analyst Phillip Hollobone at Williams de Broe. "Norwegian gas may take some time to come in but this will not help sentiment."
Hollobone said the news highlighted the pressures on both sides of British Gas's business, with the pipeline transmission side already poised to come under MMC scrutiny.

Adding to concern over the MMC inquiry, a report in the Observer newspaper said Ofgas head Clare Spottiswoode is poised to ask the MMC to widen its investigation into British Gas, to take in its trading and supply business as well as the pricing regime for its pipeline business Transco.
The newspaper said this would add to uncertainty overhanging British Gas and jeopardise its demerger plans.
A spokesman for Ofgas said the Observer report was "speculation" and said its referral to the MMC would not be formulated until the end of the week for submission to the Commission next Monday.
Hollobone said he would not be surprised to see British Gas shares retest their lows of around 175p, reached in May after initial price cut proposals for Transco from Ofgas.
"Some holders are still very reluctant to sell although I believe there are better opportunities in other utilities which offer a higher yield and better dividends," Hollobone said.
Another analyst, who asked not to be named, said the threat of Norwegian gas imports was still some way off and the more immediate concern remained the MMC inquiry.

"It means you can't reach any logical conclusions about the stock and there will be uncertainty over the next six months," the analyst said. "The polite expression is that it is just dead money. People don't hate it, they just don't want to buy it."
-- David Holmes and Hans de Jong
